subject: Autoscale buffer, burst billing, and SLA addendum for Apollo Labs

Subject: Clarify autoscale buffer / burst billing for Dedicated

Evelyn — thanks for the call earlier. We have two follow-ups from the internal cost/ops team before we can sign the Dedicated contract: 1) what exactly counts as 'burst' vs committed usage (we expect a few weekly spikes from our nightly batch jobs); 2) how will that be billed and capped; and 3) is there a way to guarantee a pre-warm window so our tail latencies don't spike during a traffic surge?

Attached is our usage forecast for the next 12 months — the spike columns are highlighted. We need a succinct addendum that maps how Redwood will handle burst capacity and the failure modes (fallback to smaller models, queueing, or rejecting requests). Can you send a short, prescriptive proposal we can pass to procurement?

Thanks,
Amira Khan
Head of ML Platform
Apollo Labs

From: Evelyn Hart <evelyn_hart@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Clarify autoscale buffer / burst billing for Dedicated

Amira — appreciate the forecast. Quick summary / proposal below (high level so procurement has something to chew on):

1) Committed vs burst: Committed capacity = reserved GPU slab defined in the contract (example: 20x A100-equivalent slots). Burst capacity = ephemeral pool used when committed is saturated. Bursts are explicitly time-limited and subject to available cluster headroom.

2) Billing & caps: Burst consumption is billed separately at a tiered overage rate. Proposal: first 10% over committed monthly usage billed at baseline rate, next 20% billed at 1.25x baseline, any additional burst billed at 1.5x baseline. We can cap monthly burst billing at an agreed % (e.g., 50% of committed monthly spend) to limit exposure — let me know if Procurement wants a hard cap.

3) Pre-warm / tail-latency: We can provide a pre-warm window (configurable) for scheduled batch runs and for predictable traffic windows. For unplanned surges we offer: (a) pre-warmed ephemeral nodes when policy triggers, (b) fallback to a smaller model variant (auto-rollover) + async queueing for low-priority requests, or (c) reject requests once soft latency SLOs are violated (only with explicit acceptance).

I've asked Ben and Karthik to add the operational constraints (headroom targets, autoscale cadence) and a short SLA addendum draft — will attach in next email. If Procurement wants an explicit charge cap, say so and we'll bake into the addendum.

Cheers,
Evelyn Hart

Subject: Re: Clarify autoscale buffer / burst billing for Dedicated

Hi all — adding the realistic operational knobs and failure modes so everyone has the same expectations. High level bullets below, keeping procurement-friendly language.

- Headroom target: We recommend a 20% maintained headroom (by instance count) across the dedicated pool to enable fast cold-start mitigation. This translates to reserving an additional transient capacity buffer on top of the committed slabs.

- Autoscale cadence: 30s evaluation loop for request-driven scaling; 5m stabilization window for node allocation to avoid thrashing. Horizontal scale increments of 2 nodes (or equivalent vGPU slices).

- Burst pool characteristics: ephemeral nodes run on spare cluster capacity (same region). They are preemptible from a physical host scheduling perspective; when reclaimed, we route to the next-best option (smaller model or queued processing).

- Pre-warm policy: scheduled pre-warm via API (customer-scheduled windows) with a 10–60 min pre-warm lead time. For detected surges we can pre-warm a small buffer (up to 10% of committed) automatically before spinning larger ephemeral nodes.

- Billing mapping (ops-friendly): we will meter GPU-seconds for committed vs ephemeral. The billing tiers Evelyn proposed are reasonable; operationally we enforce a monthly spend cap if Customer provides a PO with cap value. Alerts will be sent at 50%/80%/100% of the cap.

- SLO degradation ladder: 1) route to smaller model variant (no billing change), 2) queue non-critical requests (delayed billing at lower rate), 3) reject with a 429-like response (customer-configurable).

I'll attach a short draft addendum that spells out these knobs and the fallback flow for redline.

Ben Carter
Infrastructure & Customer Reliability
Redwood Inference

Amira — small presales note to help Procurement with definitions (copy/paste friendly):

Definitions (for contract):
- "Committed Capacity": reserved GPU capacity allocated to Customer under the contract term, billed monthly at committed rates.
- "Ephemeral/Burst Capacity": temporary capacity allocated when Committed Capacity is saturated. Ephemeral capacity is billed as overage and is subject to availability and the monthly cap.
- "Pre-warm Window": a customer-scheduled period where ephemeral capacity is provisioned ahead of expected demand; pre-warm charges are applied as ephemeral usage.

Operational guarantees (SLA addendum excerpt):
- Availability SLO for Committed Capacity: 99.9% monthly for the committed pool.
- Burst availability: best-effort; Redwood will make commercially reasonable efforts to allocate ephemeral capacity but cannot guarantee physical host availability during simultaneous large cloud-wide events.

Example billing scenario (for the deal):
- Committed: 30 GPU-month equivalent (baseline).
- April usage: committed consumed 100%, ephemeral used 25% -> first 10% at baseline, next 15% at 1.25x; monthly cap applied at 50% of committed monthly spend.

If this looks good I'll send a redlined PDF back with the formal language Procurement wants to include into Section 6 (Billing & Capacity) and Section 9 (SLOs & Fallback).

—Karthik
Principal Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference

Evelyn / team — appreciate the clarity. Procurement reviewed and wants two small changes before legal signs: 1) make the monthly burst cap a hard cap (not just an option) and put the cap value as a contract variable; 2) include a clause that for scheduled pre-warm windows Redwood will provide a 24-hour cancellation window without billing and a 2-hour window for late cancellations billed at 50% of pre-warm ephemeral cost.

If you can incorporate those two changes into the addendum and send a DocuSign link, we can aim to execute this week. Also confirm: will burst capacity failures (i.e., no ephemeral available) trigger the smaller-model fallback automatically or will that require customer opt-in? We want automatic fallback as the default.

Samir Desai
VP, Infrastructure Engineering
Apollo Labs
